paras: The Marion election riot was a shooting at the polls at Marion Station, Lauderdale County, Mississippi, on election day, November 8, 1881, followed that afternoon by a sheriff's posse's siege of the house of Ed Vance, a white Republican, where Black men had taken refuge. Four white men died of the shooting at the polls; at the house the posse killed Vance's son John, lost one of its own men and fired on fleeing Black men, with reports of Black dead ranging from none to fifteen. Wire reports blamed armed Black men, while Republican papers printed accounts in which white Democrats began the attack.

Marion lay about five miles north of Meridian, the county seat, and a National Republican correspondent called it the only Republican precinct in a "hopelessly Democratic" county. The wires described Ed Vance as the acknowledged leader of the county's Republican party.

According to the first Associated Press dispatch from Meridian, Black men "opened fire on the whites at the polls" while the whites were unarmed. Killed were A. T. Harvey, the Democratic candidate for assessor, Joseph Barnett, Jeff Segars and Vincent Segars, who died November 12; Levi Moore and James Hodges were wounded. A fuller AP account said Frank Johnson shot Barnett after a quarrel, and that George Johnson, a Black man, was fatally shot while defending Barnett.

Republican sources disagreed. A Marion letter to the Mobile Gazette said Barnett clubbed Sam Gillespie for refusing to hand over his ballot and that a Segars fired first, and a New York Times correspondent wrote that white men chased the Black men, shooting, before they turned and fired.

Sheriff R. L. Henderson brought a posse of 75 or about 100 men to Vance's house, about two miles away, after a first party under a deputy had been driven off. In the wire version, John Vance rode up pointing a gun and was shot dead, and posse member A. G. Warren was killed by a shot from the house. Will Vance was wounded and jailed, while Ed Vance and thirty or forty Black men escaped to the woods under fire, several of them wounded.

Martin Malone, a Black man, was jailed by November 10, and four more Black men were arrested on November 18 and 19, three of them at Vance's gin house. Ed Vance remained at large into December, when an anonymous letter warned the "colored route agents" at Meridian to resign or "find trouble."

After a continuance moved by Col. Horn of the Meridian Mercury, Will Vance's hearing opened at Meridian on December 22, described as a murder trial by one paper and as a preliminary examination for accessory to murder by another. Some witnesses said Will Vance cried "Go ahead, boys," while others testified that Barnett had struck Gillespie and that Segars and Harvey carried pistols. The court adjourned on December 24 pending a bail motion; no verdict, and no charge against any member of the posse, appears in the coverage.
When the hearing resumed, testimony on December 27 showed that Bob Brown, a Black man, had died about a week after the riot of wounds from the sheriff's posse, received "while resisting arrest."

The Meridian wire ran on November 9 from Cheyenne to Memphis, and the Chicago Tribune set it under the headline "The Mississippi Plan Working Badly This Evening." Mississippi Democratic papers headlined "Murderous Mokes" led "by a vile white man," and the Meridian Mercury wrote that "negro rule" would be averted "if it costs blood."

Republican papers contested the story from the first day, when the New-York Tribune called the dispatch "a Bourbon fabrication." The Daily Republican urged "several grains of allowance" and later ran the Times correspondent's version as "A Shot Gun Story Spoiled." The National Republican printed the Mobile Gazette letter as "The Colored Version" and the hearing as "The Farce of Trying Republicans."

Reports of Black dead ranged from fifteen in a Jackson dispatch to none known in the AP account. Republican accounts named George Johnson sr., an old man killed at the house, or "a number" shot as they fled. Estimates of the men in the house fell from about a hundred in the first wire to only the Vances, a white friend and one old Black man in the Times correspondent's version. A Chicago Tribune summary said Ed Vance was jailed, but later Meridian reports said he had not been found.

reader.title: Marion election riot
bases: The violence against Black people on which the accounts converge is a sheriff's posse of 75-100 armed men besieging the Vance house, where Black men had taken refuge, and firing on them as they fled (A3, A12, A28); the preceding shooting at the polls is a contested election riot (A1, A23, A26).

The polls shooting, the posse siege and the names of the white dead are corroborated by independent Meridian wires and Mississippi papers (A3, A9, A12), but Republican accounts contradict who began the shooting, how many Black men were at the house and how many were killed (A23, A26, A28).

accounts.label: First AP wire (Meridian, Nov. 8)
accounts.gist: Armed Black men opened fire on unarmed whites at the polls, killing four; about a hundred barricaded themselves in the house of their leader Ed Vance and fired on the sheriff's posse.

accounts.label: AP recapitulation (Meridian, Nov. 10)
accounts.gist: A Black man insulted Barnett and Frank Johnson shot him; named Black men did the shooting at Will Vance's urging; at the house John Vance was shot as he aimed a gun and Warren was shot from inside; no Black men known killed.

accounts.label: Marion letter to the Mobile Gazette ('The Colored Version')
accounts.gist: Barnett demanded Gillespie's ticket and clubbed him, Segars began shooting, and Black men returned fire; the Black men then sheltered at the Republican Vance's house, where John Vance and George Johnson sr. were killed.

accounts.label: New York Times correspondent
accounts.gist: A drunken Barnett struck a Black man, and white men chased the Black men shooting before they turned and fired; the house held only the four Vances, a Democratic friend and an old Black man, and the posse killed John Vance and the old man.

accounts.label: National Republican Meridian correspondent (Dec. 10)
accounts.gist: Barnett and the Segars brothers led armed whites against Black voters and Segars fired first; a few Black men from Vance's place took refuge with him, and a number of them were shot and killed fleeing the posse.

accounts.label: Prosecution witnesses at the Vance hearing
accounts.gist: Witnesses said the Vances conferred with armed Black men and Will Vance cried 'Go ahead, boys'; others said Barnett tore up Gillespie's ticket and struck him, and that Segars and Harvey had pistols.

framing.detail: Mississippi Democratic papers headlined 'Murderous Mokes' led by 'a vile white man' and cheered the capture of 'Six barrel Coders' as 'the good work'.
Northern and Western dailies ran the Meridian AP wire blaming Black men, under headlines such as 'The Mississippi Plan Working Badly' and 'War of Races'.
The New-York Tribune called the first dispatch a 'Bourbon fabrication'; the Daily Republican advised 'grains of allowance' and later ran 'A Shot Gun Story Spoiled'.
The National Republican headlined 'The Colored Version', 'The Bottom Facts of the Mississippi Massacre... The Work of Bourbon Devils' and 'The Farce of Trying Republicans'.
